s06a.slug: TUESDAY · 12:20 PM · MORRO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Oceanography 1 is two hundred people in raked seats in Morro 1100, and by eleven on Tuesday it’s safe to assume all of them have seen it. A kid in row nine hums the hook at them as they come down the side aisle, falsetto included, and three rows laugh. Fenner lets it go until he has the refraction diagram up — a long swell out of the northwest in yellow chalk, bending around a headland — and then he turns from the board with the chalk still up, finds them in the back row under the exit sign, and says, “Pair forty-one, *please*,” and the room loses it. Jack puts his forehead down on the fold-out desk. Beside him Skye uncaps a pen and copies the diagram into the margin of her notes, crest by crest, each one bending a little more than the last as it feels the bottom, and doesn’t look up until she has the final wave wrapped around the Point.

“It slows down in the shallow part,” she says, when he lifts his head. “So it turns toward it. Everything bends toward the shallow end.” She underlines it. “Fenner thinks that’s oceanography. It’s the internet.”

Morro lets out down its front steps into a hard, clean noon: backpacks, a longboard under somebody’s arm, a girl walking and eating an apple. Skye stops on the fourth step with her sunglasses in her hand and lets the class go around her like she’s a rock in a creek.
On the walk over from Delgado he gave her Ma’s call — Rita Pallante and the grandson and Father Dom’s secretary — and she made him do Rita twice. Now it’s her turn.

“Corinne called at six,” she says. “Debbie called at six-oh-four. Debbie doesn’t call. Debbie has people for calling.” She holds her iPhone up at him: a gossip site he’s never heard of, pink banner, a still of the two of them at the light with her mouth wide open on a note. *SWEETWATER’S GOOD GIRL GONE WILD?* “With a question mark. The question mark is working very hard.” She puts the phone against her chest. “The network wants to know if Cassidy is still Cassidy. They’re using the word *brand*. In a sentence. About me.”

“Cassidy,” she says, “would have sung a hymn at that light. In harmony. And the light would’ve turned green out of respect.” She hooks a finger through his belt loop to keep him on her step while a pack of lacrosse players goes by in their pinnies. “I’m not Cassidy. Cassidy is four writers and a lighting guy. I just stand where they put the tape.”
“What’s Corinne saying?”

“Corinne’s saying it’s an *unauthorized clip*.” She does it in Corinne’s mouth, every consonant filed. “She said it to me four times so I’d learn it. Like somebody bootlegged a concert.” The sunglasses go on. “Then she asked me if I regretted it, and I said I’d get back to her.”
She looks out past the bike racks at the lagoon, bright and still, a couple of pelicans standing around on the sandbar with nothing to do.
“There are hundreds of hours of me on tape, Jack. Hours. If the building was on fire I’d go back in for those thirty-eight seconds.”
He looks at her. She posts everything — the taco photo, a sunset at the Rincon, a menu she disagrees with — and this morning there is nothing about it on her page at all.
“You didn’t put it up.”

“Your mother’s secretary’s priest has seen it, Jack.” She has the chain slightly wrong, and it doesn’t slow her down. “I’m not putting it on a plate for them. Some girl in a Jetta put it up without asking. That’s on her. I don’t do that to you on purpose.” She turns the iPhone around. “This, I did on purpose.”

body.name: Skye Callender
body.text: looking forward to our next singalong. bring the clean version next time, for everybody watching at home

body: It’s on his wall. Not hers: his, where Gina and Tommy Hritz and Mrs. Pallante’s grandson can see it, under his own name, a few hours after her publicist started calling it unauthorized. It’s a wink at Youngstown, and it says, in front of everybody, that she was there on purpose and would go again.
“Corinne called back at nine-fifteen,” Skye says. “I let it ring. It was very freeing.”

The kid from row nine comes down the steps past them, walking backward so he can point. “Forty-one!” Then, still backing: “Wait. Are you also the guy from the professor’s house? Somebody said the dog needed stitches.”
“The dog’s fine,” Jack says.

The kid takes this with him down the steps. Skye watches him go and says, “Debbie wants me to do a sit-down with a magazine about my *journey*,” and goes on with Debbie, and the dog is not mentioned again.
Jack watches her talk. Her mother’s six-oh-four. A network that bought a nice girl and wants her back. A word like *brand* said about her over breakfast. He did that, at a red light, with a lime.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does. Saturday at the Point with Fenner’s form and a stopwatch, timing the sets. Skye called the surfers like the last hole of a golf tournament. Breaking where it does. Tuesday two hundred people had seen it. Fenner said Pair forty-one, *please*, and the room lost it. Skye was doing his refraction diagram in the margin.

journal.title: Corinne Waxman
journal.text: Corinne Waxman. Skye’s publicist. Answers the phone with her own name. Reads a BlackBerry the way other people read a room; uses a legal pad only when a lawyer might read it later. Ran my name in January. Tuesday she read the *Vindicator* off it, and asked me, kindly, what happened. Wrote down Danny’s number when Skye said it. Thursday: a fundraiser in the Palisades. It’s civic. Thursday she wanted the arrival picture on Skye’s page; she got tacos and a caption. She stopped typing for most of the argument. She says I was supposed to be furniture. The host’s office called her twice: Gil wants us both back in the spring. The taco picture is sweet, she says, and sweet isn’t a strategy. Tuesday she called Skye at six. The clip is unauthorized, she says. Skye wrote on my wall anyway.

choices.text: “I cost you something today. I’m sorry.”
choices.key: On the Morro steps you told Skye you were sorry for what the video cost her. She kissed you in front of the whole class and told you never to apologize for making her happy.
response: “I cost you something today,” he says. “I’m sorry.”

She looks at him over the top of the sunglasses. Then she puts the phone in her back pocket, and her hands come up under his jaw, cold from the rail, and she kisses him slow and hard on the fourth step of Morro Hall with the class parting around them on both sides, long enough that the parting turns into a detour.
“Don’t ever apologize to me for making me happy,” she says against his mouth.
Two steps down, the kid from row nine starts to applaud by himself, gets three claps in, and stops.

choices.text: “I’m sorry. Your job — your mother — I’m sorry.”
choices.key: On the Morro steps you apologized to Skye for her job and her mother. She kissed you in front of the whole class and told you never to apologize for making her happy.
response: “I’m sorry,” he says. “Your job — your mother —”

She stops him at *mother* with both hands on his face, and kisses him, slow and hard, standing a step above him so she doesn’t have to reach. Somebody coming down the rail says *excuse me* and then, closer, *oh, excuse me*.
“Never apologize for making me happy,” she says. “Not to me. Not ever.”
Her thumbs stay on his cheekbones after, pressing a little, like she’s smoothing down tape on something she wants to keep.

choices.text: “I’d like to formally apologize to the network.”
choices.key: On the Morro steps you offered to apologize to her network. She kissed you in front of the whole class and told you never to apologize for making her happy.
response: “I’d like to formally apologize to the network,” he says. “On behalf of the Mahoning Valley.”
She laughs, and then she takes his face in her hands and isn’t laughing at all, and kisses him slow and hard, the sunglasses knocked crooked against his cheekbone and left there.
“The network can have a statement,” she says. “You never apologize for making me happy.”
Behind her the doors open and Fenner comes out with his coffee and his handouts, steps around the two of them on the fourth step, and goes on down toward the lagoon, reading.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING
body: The swing hangs at Sol’s again, the old driftwood seat on new galvanized chain that still creaks like a pair of new shoes whenever anybody shifts. Below the bluff the surf is big and left over from some storm up by Alaska, and the sun has started down the back half of the afternoon toward the Point. Skye has her knees up inside his flannel and her bare feet on the front edge of the seat. Her iPhone is face down on the boards where she dropped it, and it has been buzzing since he sat down — Corinne, every couple of minutes, the phone walking itself across the wood toward the steps until Skye puts out a heel and shoves it back under the swing, where it goes on buzzing against the boards.

The RAZR goes off on his knee. On the little outside screen, a long 330 number he has never saved and would know in his sleep. 3:40 here, 6:40 in Leavittsburg: after count, after chow, his brother’s turn at the wall.

He opens it. The recording comes on loud enough for the porch. “This is a prepaid call from —” and into the gap, fast, his brother’s own voice: “Danny.” “— an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution. This call is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept, press one.”
Jack presses one.
“Professor.”
“Happy birthday, Dan.”

“This is recorded, so everybody keep it clean,” Danny says. “Hi, State of Ohio.” Behind him, a hallway: a TV turned up for a room, a door that bangs on a spring. “Twenty-three. Old enough to know better. Ain’t stopped me yet. Called the house this morning, caught Ma with her coat on, so this one’s yours. Two calls. I’m living large.” A breath. “Your card ain’t come. Gina’s came. She drew a candle on it. Late’s a Costigan tradition.”
“Pop’s never been on time to anything but a shift.”
Danny laughs, the short one. “He was early to those. Twenty-six years, he was early.”

body.text: “Your girl’s letter came. In capitals. Nobody writes me in capitals but my sister and the State of Ohio.” Beside him Skye puts both hands over her mouth.
body.else: “Your girl says she wrote. I’m holding her to it.” Beside him Skye puts a hand over her eyes.

body.text: Before Danny can get to the song, Jack says it. “It was for you, Dan.” “Ma ain’t gonna tell me that,” Danny says. “Ma’s gonna take that to her grave and then tell St. Peter.”

body: “So Ma wouldn’t say the name of it,” Danny says. “On my *birthday*, Professor. She said there’s a video and a song she won’t say, and then she said happy birthday like she was reading it off a sympathy card. What’d you *sing*?”

body.text: “I stood up in the car,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.
“I did the high part,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.
“I sang it at her,” Jack says, which isn’t the question.

body: Skye has been listening with her chin on her knees. Now she unfolds one arm out of the flannel and holds out her hand to him and crooks her fingers twice. “Give me him.”
He gives her him. She hits the speaker key like she’s done it on a RAZR all her life and sets the phone on her knee, face up. “I want you to hear this,” she tells Jack.
“Hello?” says Trumbull, suspicious.
“Danny,” she says. “Happy birthday. It’s Skye.”
“So you’re the one,” Danny says, warm as anything, out of Leavittsburg. “What’d you lose the bet for?”
“Danny. Danny.” She puts a hand on her heart. “There was no bet. There was an *operation*.”
And she tells him the trick.

It starts in October, with a recall notice under her wiper: General Motors letterhead, very official, very creased. Her Saab, which is a GM car — “look it up, Danny, he made me look it up” — “It’s a GM car,” Danny agrees — has a defect in what the notice calls the emotional transmission, and the only man in California certified to repair it is a specialist from Lordstown. Enter Jack, in coveralls, with his name sewn over the pocket. “What name?” Danny says. “*Jack*. In cursive. He did it himself. Badly.”

He needed a man on the inside, so he bribed his roommate with a Browns hat. “The rich one took a *Browns* hat?” “The *rich* one,” Skye says, delighted. “Is that what you call him? I call him Ted. Yours is so much better.” Ted, she explains, would sell her to a circus for a hat; Ted has a hat problem; Ted got her address.

There is a woman at a diner on the harbor who rates men by pie. So Jack’s grandmother mailed a Calabrese love spell out to California in a coffee can, and it went into the crust. “It’s in the *crust*, Danny. That’s why he’s lattice-top.” “What’s lattice-top?” “Pretty on top. Everything’s leaking underneath.” “That’s him,” Danny says. “That’s him *exactly*.”

After that he came to her door as a Bible salesman, in a hat, with a sample case, and the Bible was hollow — “like in the story, Danny, he reads the stories, he knew *exactly* what he was doing” — and inside the hollow Bible was —
“Ma’am,” Danny says, “the State of Ohio is *listening*.”
“— a coupon,” Skye says. “For pie.”

That’s where Danny goes. It’s the big one, the laugh Jack gets maybe once a visit, that starts somewhere under Danny’s ribs and takes all the air out of him on the way up, and it comes out of the little speaker on her knee so loud the chain creaks with her flinching. Somewhere behind it a man’s voice, bored and far off, says *Costigan, keep it down.* Danny, with the phone away from his mouth: “Sorry, sir — family news.”

Skye doesn’t wait for him. There was an actor hired to play a priest and tell her it was God’s will — “I know actors, Danny, the man couldn’t kneel, he went down like a card table” — and a permission slip, signed by the Pope, in green ink. “Which Pope?” “The current one, Danny, I’m not an *animal*.” And there was the book. Jack had operatives plant a paperback Flannery O’Connor in a den in Montecito, open to the grandmother, and wait in the shrubbery for her to sit down beside it.
“He did that to a girl in eighth grade,” Danny says, wheezing, “with a Pontiac.”
“*Which* girl.”
“I’ll send you a list.”

She’s pushing the swing off the boards with her toes on the funny parts and letting it come back by itself. She laughs at her own story before she gets to the end of her sentences and doesn’t care whether the end lands; her eyes are out on the water, not on him. He has watched her be funny all winter — for a fundraiser in the Palisades, for Gloria at the Anchor, for Corinne, for him — and every time some piece of her was standing at the back of the room minding the angle; this afternoon there is no room, only a porch and a prison phone and a man in Leavittsburg she has never laid eyes on, and as far as Jack can tell she is doing it for nothing but the sound of him laughing.
“And you want to know *why*, Danny?” she says. “The coveralls. The hat. The *Pope*.”
“Why.”
“He was out of stamps. He needed somebody else to write you.”
Jack puts his face in his hands. In Leavittsburg his brother makes a noise like a man falling down a flight of stairs on purpose.
It takes Danny some time to come back. When he does he is wheezing, and his voice is smaller and nearer the phone. “Okay. Okay.” A breath that rattles. “What’d he really do.”
Skye stops the swing with her heel.

“The Friday before Thanksgiving,” she says. “A house in Montecito. A boy named Wyatt Halloran whose parents were in London. I didn’t know anybody. I was in the window seat in the den, because it was the one place in that house nobody could stand behind me. I had a paperback of *A Good Man Is Hard to Find* and a Sharpie, because I was reading for a preacher’s daughter who forgives a boy in the rain, and I’d decided the grandmother was a liar. I wrote LIAR in the margin next to her. Three times. Bigger every time.”
She pulls the flannel tighter over her knees.
“I had one boot on, Danny. I was leaving.”
Jack’s hand on the chain stops.

“And this guy comes across the room. Borrowed shirt — it was Ted’s, I didn’t know that yet. He didn’t know who I was. He didn’t care who I was. He crossed the den by himself to tell me I had the grandmother backwards. So I argued, and he argued back, and he was good, and he was annoying, and I asked him the thing I couldn’t figure out — at the end, when she reaches out and touches the man with the gun, what does she *want*? Because everybody in every scene wants something. That’s the job.” She stops, and starts again. “And he said, ‘Nothing. That’s the point. For one second she doesn’t want anything from anybody. That’s what grace looks like from the outside. And he can’t stand it.’”
The surf comes in under the bluff and goes out.

“I had PLAY IT AS A CON at the bottom of the page,” she says. “And I crossed out CON. In my own margin. I’ve never crossed out a note in my life, Danny. Notes are how I get paid.” He can see her take the boot back off, in the den, in November. “Then I drove him up the coast to a beach of mine and dared him into the Pacific in his clothes, and he emptied his pockets onto my boots and walked into the Pacific in his jeans one step at a time like it was a procession, and I called him Coat check, and he’s been Coat check since. And we talked till it got gray.”

“You want to know when I decided to kiss him? Around the grandmother’s hand on the Misfit’s shoulder. Two and a half hours before I asked. And then when I finally asked, he didn’t let me finish.” She breathes out. “I still have the book. It’s on my nightstand. CON’s still crossed out.”
Jack has slept six feet from that nightstand and never once looked at what was on it.
“That’s what he did,” Skye says, very quietly. “He didn’t want anything from me. All night. He just wanted me to be right about the grandmother.”
The chain is cold under his hand. He keeps hold of it.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told Danny what really happened in Montecito. You took her hand.
response: He lets go of the chain and finds her hand on the slats by her hip. She turns it over to meet his before he gets there, and laces her fingers through his, and grips hard enough to hurt a little.

choices.text: *Tell her that’s not how you remember it. It was better.*
choices.key: On the swing Skye told Danny what really happened in Montecito. You told her it was better than that.
response: “That’s not how I remember it,” he says, low, not for the phone. “It was better.”
She turns her head on her knees and looks at him like he’s changed a line on her in the middle of a take, and she lets him have it.

choices.key: On the swing Skye told Danny what really happened in Montecito. You told her she left out *Rumours*.
response: “Danny doesn’t need to know about the Fleetwood Mac,” she says, wet-eyed and perfectly steady. “It’s a federal facility.”

choices.key: On the swing Skye told Danny what really happened in Montecito. You said nothing and let her finish.
response: He keeps his mouth shut and his hand on the chain, and there is one more sentence, about the light coming up gray behind the oil platforms, and she says it to her own knees.

s07a.slug: TUESDAY · 3:53 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH — THE SWING

body.text: Her hand is in his on the seat, warm and tight, and on the phone, nothing.
She’s still looking at him, and on the phone, nothing.
“State facility,” she repeats, to herself, and on the phone, nothing.
Her last sentence goes out over the porch rail toward the water, and on the phone, nothing.

body: Just the hiss of the line, and a long way behind it the TV for somebody else’s room and a door banging on its spring. It goes on long enough that Jack leans to look at the little screen to see if the call has dropped. The seconds are still counting.
Danny coughs. It goes on too long for a cough.
“Lady,” he says, when he has it back down, “I’m in *prison*. You can’t do that to me in *here*.”
Skye laughs, and it comes out wet, and she wipes under one eye with the cuff of the flannel.
“*Professor*,” Danny says.
Just that.
The recording cuts in over it, the same flat woman. “You have one minute remaining.”
Skye picks the RAZR up off her knee with both hands and holds it close. “Call me,” she says into it. “Call *us*. I’ll be the one who answers.”

body.text: “Yeah. Yeah, I’ll call.” A breath. “You keep that phone charged, Mary Catherine.”
body.else: “Yeah. Yeah, I’ll call. You keep that phone charged.”

body.text: At the name she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut till she has the phone back on her knee.

body: She puts it in Jack’s hand, still on speaker, and stays against his shoulder, close enough to hear the line breathing. He leans down to it.
“She’s the one I can tell the truth to.”
“Yeah, I can tell, Professor. You’re not subtle. I’m still going with the trick though, easier to wrap my brain around that one.”

The line clicks. On the little screen the call timer stops, and then it says CALL ENDED, and then it’s only the time. After that it’s the porch: the surf under the bluff, a car going by slow on Del Playa with its windows down, the new chains.
Jack sits with the dead phone open in his hand. The swing goes on moving a little by itself, the way it does after somebody gets off it, except nobody has.
Skye takes the RAZR out of his hand, folds it shut, and gives it back to him.
“He laughs like you,” she says. “When you forget to be careful.”
Under the swing the iPhone starts up against the boards again. She lets it go three buzzes before she reaches down for it, turns it over, and answers it without looking at the name.
“Not now, Corinne. I’m at a birthday.”
She hangs up, drops it in the flannel’s front pocket, puts her feet to the boards, and pushes off, and they swing.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas, his twenty-third, he called from Trumbull and got Skye. My card hadn’t come. Gina’s had, with a candle on it. Skye’s letter came, in capitals. Ma wouldn’t tell him the name of the song. Skye told him how I tricked her — a long caper, a love spell in Gloria’s crust — and he laughed till they told him to keep it down. Family news, he said. Then she told him what really happened in Montecito, and he coughed for a while. She asked him to call again. I told him she’s the one I can tell the truth to. He said I’m not subtle. He’s still going with the trick.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out.
